arrangements.name: One step further
arrangements.summary: Same chords as the score. The arpeggio reaches a tenth, and the left hand rolls in eighths whenever the melody holds a long note.
tips: Practise the left hand alone at tempo 60 until the reach from the fifth to the tenth feels relaxed.
In measures 7 and 15 the melody stands still, so let the left hand sing there and keep it quiet elsewhere.

patterns.name: Tenth arpeggio
patterns.description: Root, fifth, then the third one octave up instead of the root. One changed note makes the chord sound open and warm.

patterns.name: Rolling eighths
patterns.description: Climb through the chord in eighth notes and turn back at the top. Use it while the melody holds a long note.

measures.note: Tenth arpeggio: the last note is 3' instead of 1'.
Your usual pattern, so the new one stands out against it.
The melody holds one note for five beats, so the left hand takes over the movement.
The seventh (7) appears inside the roll and pulls towards G.
Ending on the seventh leads the ear into the C chord.
Single notes only: bass D, then B rising to C, which falls back to B in the last chord.
Close with all three notes together.

arrangements.name: Walking bass
arrangements.summary: A waltz texture: one bass note, then two notes together. Inversions let the bass move by step instead of jumping from root to root.
tips: Play only the first note of every measure and listen to the bass line as a melody of its own.
Keep the two-note chords lighter than the bass note.

patterns.name: Bass and pair
patterns.description: Bass note on the first beat, fifth and octave together on the other beats.

patterns.name: Slash-chord bass
patterns.description: Keep the same pair on top and put the third of the chord in the bass. G/B sits one step below C, so the bass walks.

measures.note: G/B: the bass steps up from G through B to reach C in the next measure.
The bass steps back down from C to B.
Em replaces G: it shares two notes with G, and its bass E walks down to D.
D7/C puts the seventh in the bass. It wants to fall one step, to the B of G/B.
The bass stays on B while the pair changes to include the seventh.
The bass walks E to D and stays there; the last pair holds the two notes that define D7.

arrangements.name: New chords
arrangements.summary: Several printed chords are replaced: a secondary dominant, a suspended chord that resolves, and an Amen ending.
tips: Learn the shell shape 1 7 3' on Em7 first; the A7 in the next measure uses exactly the same shape.
Listen for the single note that moves when Dsus4 turns into D7.

patterns.name: Shell voicing
patterns.description: Root, seventh, and the third one octave up. Three notes are enough to show the whole colour of a seventh chord.

patterns.name: Suspend, then resolve
patterns.description: Hold back the third of the dominant by playing the fourth, then let it fall one step.

patterns.name: Amen ending
patterns.description: Place the IV chord over the home bass note before the final chord, the way a sung Amen closes a hymn.

measures.note: G7/B turns the home chord into a dominant of C and puts the leading note B in the bass.
Em7 stands in for G. The melody notes G and B both belong to it.
A7 is the dominant of D, the chord that follows. The hand shape is the same as in the previous measure.
Dsus4 delays the arrival: the fourth (G) replaces the third.
The suspended G falls to F sharp and the chord finally sounds complete.
The bass arrives home on G, but the chord above is still C. The real ending waits one more measure.
The Amen resolves.
